sections.h2: Which part of central Ohio does Licking County cover?
sections.html:
Licking County sits in central Ohio, with Newark as the county seat. Wikipedia says the legislature created it from part of Fairfield County on January 30, 1808, and that it was organized on March 1, 1808. It covers about 683 square miles of land, which makes it the third-largest Ohio county by land area, and it belongs to the Columbus metropolitan area.

Seven counties touch it: Knox, Coshocton, Muskingum, Perry, Fairfield, Franklin and Delaware. Interstate 70 and U.S. 40 are the named through routes. Six cities lie inside the county: Heath, Johnstown, New Albany, Newark, Pataskala and Reynoldsburg. Manufacturing is a large employer, with Intel, Armstrong World Industries, Invenergy and Atkore named among the investors, and farming still ranks the county 11th among Ohio's 88 counties for products sold.

That mix matters for a property tax bill. A farm parcel near Utica, a rowhouse-era lot in Newark and a new build in New Albany sit in different school, township and municipal taxing districts, so two homes with the same value can carry different bills.

sections.h2: What do Census figures show for Licking County homeowners?
sections.html:
The Census Bureau QuickFacts page for Licking County reports a county that grew from 178,501 residents in April 2020 to an estimate of 185,564 in July 2025, a rise of 4.0 percent. Housing figures for 2020 to 2024 read as follows:

  • Median value of owner-occupied homes: $275,200.
  • Owner-occupied rate: 73.7 percent, across 68,620 households.
  • Median monthly owner cost with a mortgage: $1,693. Without a mortgage: $631.
  • Median gross rent: $1,078.
  • Median household income: $84,426.
  • Housing units counted in July 2025: 73,930.

Licking County's land area is 682.43 square miles, and 66.2 percent of residents lived in areas the 2020 census classed as urban, according to Wikipedia's census summary.

sections.h2: Which Licking County offices handle property tax?
sections.html:
Two offices on the second floor of the County Administration Building at 20 South Second Street in Newark do most of the work. The auditor sets values, certifies tax rates, runs the tax reduction programs and serves as secretary to the Board of Revision. The treasurer collects real estate tax, manufactured home tax, estate tax, hotel and motel tax and special assessments.

  • Auditor: (740) 670-5040, Monday to Friday, 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM, closed on holidays.
  • Treasurer: 740-670-5010, same weekday hours.
  • Online lookup: both offices point to the county's OnTrac site for parcel search and tax information.
  • Transfers: the auditor set a 4 p.m. cutoff effective May 1, 2026 for same-day conveyances, exempt transfers, splits and merges.

The treasurer's page warns that tax payments never go to the auditor or the recorder. Send them to the treasurer only.

sections.h2: What did the 2026 triennial update do to Licking County values?
sections.html:
The auditor published a public notice, citing Ohio Revised Code 5713.01, that the 2026 Triennial Update of Licking County property values is complete. Owners can review the new values on OnTrac or at the auditor's counter between 8:30 AM and 4:30 PM on weekdays. The notice gives no percentage, so look up your own parcel to see what moved.

The Ohio Department of Taxation schedule puts Licking in the middle of a six-year cycle: an update in 2026 and the next full reappraisal in 2029. The table shows how neighboring counties line up on that same schedule.

sections.h2: When are Licking County property taxes due, and what happens if you pay late?
sections.html:
Ohio taxes are paid in two halves, and the treasurer prints the exact dates on each bill. Call 740-670-5010 or check the bill for the current installment dates, because counties can move them from year to year.

The penalty rules come from Ohio Revised Code 323.121. A missed half draws a 10 percent penalty on the unpaid balance. If the full amount arrives within ten days after the due date, the treasurer waives half of that penalty. Interest on delinquent balances is added on the first day of the month after the second-half deadline and again on December 1.

A payment counts as timely if the treasurer receives it by the last day or if the envelope carries a U.S. Postal Service postmark on or before that day. A private meter postmark does not count, per section 323.12.

sections.h2: How do you challenge a Licking County valuation?
sections.html:
File a complaint with the county auditor, who passes it to the Board of Revision. Under Ohio Revised Code 5715.19, the complaint is due by March 31 of the following tax year, or the closing date of first-half collection if that falls later. A mailed complaint is dated by its postmark.

  • Owners, spouses, qualified appraisers, accountants and licensed brokers acting for the owner may file.
  • One complaint per parcel is allowed in each interim period, unless the property sold at arm's length, lost value to a casualty, received a substantial improvement, or saw occupancy change by at least 15 percent.
  • The board must give at least ten days' notice of the hearing and decide within 180 days after the filing deadline.
  • While a complaint is pending, the treasurer must accept a payment calculated on the value the owner claims.
  • Bring all evidence to the board. Evidence withheld there can be barred on a later appeal.

Ask the auditor's office for the current complaint form and any filing instructions before you prepare the paperwork.

sections.h2: What does a seller deal with at the auditor's counter in Licking County?
sections.html:
The deed reaches the auditor before it reaches the recorder. Under section 319.202, the buyer or the buyer's representative files a statement of value, and the auditor endorses the deed with the conveyance fee charged. The statement also records whether the property received a tax reduction or farm-use valuation that could affect the buyer.

The seller pays the state-authorized conveyance fee at that stage. A county transfer tax applies only where the commissioners adopted one under section 322.02, capped at thirty cents per hundred dollars. Ask the auditor at (740) 670-5040 whether Licking County charges it. Sellers who own farmland should tell the title company early whether the parcel was ever in the agricultural use program, since recoupment is handled in the same filing.

Get the deed to the auditor before 4 p.m. on the day you want it processed. A later arrival waits for the next business day.

faqs.q: Who do I call about a Licking County tax bill?
faqs.a: Call the treasurer at 740-670-5010 for payment questions and the auditor at (740) 670-5040 for value questions. Both offices are at 20 South Second Street in Newark and keep weekday hours of 8:30 AM to 4:30 PM.

faqs.q: When is the next full reappraisal in Licking County?
faqs.a: The Ohio Department of Taxation schedule lists 2029 as the next reappraisal year for Licking County. The 2026 triennial update has already been completed.

faqs.q: Can I file a complaint every year in Licking County?
faqs.a: No, one complaint per parcel is allowed in each interim period under Ohio Revised Code 5715.19. A new complaint is allowed in that window only after an arm's length sale, a casualty loss, a substantial improvement, or a 15 percent occupancy change.

faqs.q: Does Licking County charge a transfer tax when I sell?
faqs.a: Ask the auditor, because Ohio counties adopt the optional transfer tax by commissioner resolution and the cap is thirty cents per hundred dollars. The state conveyance fee applies separately and the seller pays it at the auditor's counter.

faqs.q: What happens if I miss a Licking County tax installment?
faqs.a: A 10 percent penalty is charged on the unpaid half, and half of it is waived if you pay within ten days. Interest then runs on delinquent balances, so contact the treasurer before the next installment.
